q: Why did Rome fall but Constantinople last another thousand years?

must.pt: Constantinople's site was nearly impregnable: water on three sides and the Theodosian Walls (413) on the land side
The East had the richer, more urban tax base (Egypt, Syria, Anatolia), the West a long Rhine-Danube frontier and a poorer, rural base
The loss of North Africa to the Vandals (Carthage 439) cut the Western government's revenue and grain
The East kept a salaried army, navy and bureaucracy and could pay off or redirect invaders westward
476 is a convention: the West dissolved into successor kingdoms over decades rather than in one event

avoid: Lead poisoning or moral decadence as the main cause
Christianity as the agreed main cause

q: Why did India rarely consolidate into one state?

must.pt: The premise is only partly true: the Maurya (under Ashoka), the Delhi Sultanate under Muhammad bin Tughluq and the Mughals under Aurangzeb ruled most of the subcontinent
Geography makes several rich cores (Indus-Ganges plain, Deccan, the Tamil south, Bengal) separated by the Vindhyas, forests and distance
Big empires ruled through layered, tributary sovereignty and local intermediaries (zamindars, nayakas) rather than direct rule, so they came apart at the seams
An armed peasantry and an open military labour market made rebellion and new states cheap (Kolff)
Repeated entry of conquerors through the north-west passes (Khyber, Bolan) kept rebuilding power from the north

avoid: India was never unified before the British
Caste alone explains political fragmentation

q: Why did China keep coming back together after it broke apart?

must.pt: The Qin unification of 221 BCE standardised script, weights, coinage and law, and the shared written language outlived every dynasty
A single dominant threat from the northern steppe rewarded one large centralised state (Ko, Koyama and Sng)
The open North China Plain and the Grand Canal tied the grain of the south to the political centre in the north
An examination-recruited bureaucracy and the Confucian idea of one Mandate of Heaven made reunification the expected outcome
China was divided for long stretches too: Warring States, roughly 220-589 CE, the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms

avoid: China was always unified
Unity explained by 'Asian despotism'

q: When did Western Europe actually start to become rich?

must.pt: Sustained growth of income per head is mainly a post-1800 story; before that, gains were small and reversible
A 'Little Divergence' from about 1500-1600: the Low Countries and England pulled ahead of southern and eastern Europe (Maddison Project, Broadberry, Allen)
The Black Death raised real wages and helped make north-west Europe a high-wage economy
The Great Divergence debate: Pomeranz argues the Yangzi delta was comparable until about 1750-1800; others (Broadberry, Allen) date the gap earlier
Atlantic trade and the institutions it strengthened (Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson), and coal

avoid: Europe was richer than everyone since antiquity

q: What did the end of the world look like in 1177 BCE?

must.pt: A cluster of collapses around 1200-1150 BCE: Hittite empire and Hattusa, Ugarit (destroyed about 1185), the Mycenaean palaces and Linear B
Ramesses III's inscription at Medinet Habu (his year 8, about 1177 BCE) records fighting off the Sea Peoples
Drought and climate evidence (pollen and lake cores, e.g. Kaniewski), plus earthquakes and famine (Hittite grain requests to Egypt)
Systems collapse: interlinked palace economies depending on tin and copper trade failed together (Cline)
Egypt survived but weakened; Iron Age successors (Phoenician cities, Israelites, Neo-Hittite states) emerged

avoid: The Sea Peoples alone caused the collapse
All of it happened in the single year 1177

q: Which cities lasted for thousands of years, which vanished, and why?

must.pt: Long-lived examples on the same site: Damascus, Aleppo, Jericho or Byblos, Athens, Varanasi, Luoyang or Xi'an, Rome
Vanished examples: Uruk, Babylon, Mohenjo-daro, Angkor, Cahokia, Ctesiphon
Rivers shifting or silting and water failing killed cities (Uruk and the Euphrates, Ephesus's harbour)
Shifting trade routes and lost capital status (Petra, Palmyra) versus strategic sites that get rebuilt after every sack

q: What happened to the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World?

must.pt: Only the Great Pyramid of Giza survives
The Colossus of Rhodes fell in an earthquake about 226 BCE
The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was burned by Herostratus in 356 BCE, rebuilt, and wrecked again (Goths in 268 CE)
The Lighthouse of Alexandria was ruined by earthquakes; its stones went into the Citadel of Qaitbay (1477-80)
The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus fell to earthquakes; the Knights Hospitaller reused its stones in Bodrum Castle
The Hanging Gardens may never have existed in Babylon (Stephanie Dalley's Nineveh hypothesis)

avoid: Stating the Hanging Gardens' location as certain

q: How did the Black Death spread across Eurasia, and what did it change?

must.pt: Caused by Yersinia pestis; ancient DNA points to an origin in Central Asia (Tian Shan, Issyk-Kul graves of 1338-39)
Reached Europe via the Black Sea: Caffa about 1346, Genoese galleys to Messina in October 1347
Killed roughly 30-50% or more of Europe's people between 1347 and 1351
Afterwards real wages rose and serfdom weakened in the west while a 'second serfdom' grew in the east
Massacres of Jews blamed for the plague (Strasbourg 1349)

avoid: Rats alone stated as settled transmission
It killed half the world

q: What did the Columbian Exchange do to the Americas and the rest of the world?

must.pt: Smallpox, measles and other Old World diseases caused a catastrophic Native American population decline, by most estimates well over half
Maize, potatoes and cassava spread to Eurasia and Africa and supported population growth (Nunn and Qian on the potato)
Horses, cattle, wheat and sugar transformed the Americas (Plains horse cultures)
American silver from Potosi flowed into Europe and on to China
Pre-contact population figures are deeply uncertain (from about 8 to over 100 million)

avoid: One pre-contact population figure stated as certain

q: How did the 1918 influenza spread around the world so quickly?

must.pt: Spread in waves from 1918 to 1919, the deadly second wave in autumn 1918
First World War troop movements, camps and ships carried it
Killed roughly 50 million people (estimates range from about 17 to 100 million)
Unusually lethal for young adults (the W-shaped mortality curve)
India suffered the largest toll, on the order of 12-20 million
Called 'Spanish' only because neutral Spain's press reported it freely; its origin is unknown

avoid: Stating its origin as certain

q: Why did the Silk Road matter, and was it really one road?

must.pt: It was a shifting network of routes, named 'Seidenstraße' by Ferdinand von Richthofen in 1877
Most trade was relayed in stages; few people or goods went end to end
Sogdian merchants were key middlemen in the first millennium
Ideas travelled with goods: Buddhism into China, Manichaeism, Church of the East Christianity, paper westward
The Mongol peace revived overland trade in the 13th-14th centuries

avoid: One continuous road
Han China and Rome traded directly

q: How did the monsoon winds shape trade across the Indian Ocean?

must.pt: The monsoon reverses with the seasons, so ships sailed out on one and back on the other, setting a yearly calendar
Greco-Roman ships from Red Sea ports reached Muziris on the Malabar coast (Periplus of the Erythraean Sea)
Port cities and diasporas grew around the wind schedule: Swahili coast, Gujarat, Calicut, Malacca
Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498 using a local pilot; the Portuguese tried to control trade by force

q: How did Mali become rich, and what did Mansa Musa's pilgrimage show the world?

must.pt: Sundiata Keita founded the empire in the 13th century (Kurukan Fuga, about 1235)
Its wealth came from the gold fields of Bambuk and Bure and from taxing trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt
Timbuktu and Djenne became centres of trade and Islamic learning
Musa's hajj (1324-25) spent so much gold in Cairo that its value fell there for years (al-Umari)
The 1375 Catalan Atlas pictures Musa holding a gold nugget

avoid: 'Richest man ever' stated as fact with a dollar figure

q: How big was the Atlantic slave trade, and where did the people go?

must.pt: About 12.5 million people were embarked and about 10.7 million survived the crossing (SlaveVoyages database)
Brazil received the most, roughly 40-45%, and the Caribbean most of the rest; about 400,000 went to mainland North America
West-Central Africa (Congo-Angola) was the largest region of embarkation, then the Bight of Benin and Bight of Biafra
The trade peaked in the 18th century, driven by sugar plantations
Middle Passage mortality averaged around 12-15%

avoid: Most enslaved Africans went to the United States

q: Why was Song China so advanced, and why didn't it industrialise?

must.pt: Song (960-1279) had paper money (jiaozi), fast-ripening Champa rice and booming commerce
Northern iron output reached very high levels by about 1078 (Robert Hartwell's estimates)
Gunpowder weapons, the magnetic compass for navigation and movable type (Bi Sheng) date from the Song
Jurchen Jin took the north in 1127, the Mongols conquered the south by 1279
Competing explanations for no industrial breakthrough: high-level equilibrium trap (Elvin), coal and colonies (Pomeranz), state priorities

q: How did the Mongols build the largest contiguous land empire in history?

must.pt: Temujin was proclaimed Chinggis Khan at the 1206 kurultai after uniting the steppe tribes
Mounted archers with composite bows, decimal units, relay posts (yam) and recruited siege engineers
Rule by merit and loyalty, plus calculated terror toward cities that resisted
An unusually wet, mild period on the steppe (Pederson tree rings, 1211-25) fed the horses
By the 1260s it split into four khanates; the Yuan conquered Song China by 1279

avoid: Stating a precise peak area as certain

q: Why did Constantinople fall in 1453, and what changed afterwards?

must.pt: Mehmed II besieged the city from 6 April to 29 May 1453
Huge cannon (Orban's) and the Rumeli Hisari fortress cutting off the Bosphorus
Ottoman ships were dragged overland into the Golden Horn
Byzantium was already a tiny rump state of a few tens of thousands of people
Istanbul became the Ottoman capital; Greek scholars took manuscripts to Italy, a contribution to (not the cause of) the Renaissance

avoid: 1453 alone caused the European voyages of discovery

q: How did a few hundred Spaniards bring down the Aztec Empire?

must.pt: Tlaxcala and other Indigenous allies supplied tens of thousands of warriors: it was largely an Indigenous war
Smallpox struck Tenochtitlan in 1520, killing Cuitlahuac
The Triple Alliance's tribute system made many subject cities willing to switch sides
The 1521 siege used brigantines on Lake Texcoco and cut the causeways and water supply
Malintzin (La Malinche) was interpreter and negotiator

avoid: The Aztecs thought Cortes was the god Quetzalcoatl (stated as fact)
Guns alone won it

q: How did the Inca run an empire without writing or markets?

must.pt: Khipu knotted cords recorded census, tribute and possibly narratives
Labour tax (mit'a) instead of money taxes, with goods kept in state storehouses (qollqa)
The Qhapaq Nan road network (roughly 30,000-40,000 km) with chasqui relay runners
Rapid expansion under Pachacuti from about 1438; the 1532 Spanish arrival came during the Atahualpa-Huascar civil war, after smallpox

avoid: No writing means no records

q: Why did a murder in Sarajevo start a world war?

must.pt: Gavrilo Princip shot Archduke Franz Ferdinand on 28 June 1914
The July Crisis: Germany's 'blank cheque', the Austro-Hungarian ultimatum to Serbia, Russian mobilisation
Two alliance blocs (Triple Entente, Central Powers) turned a Balkan war into a continental one
The Schlieffen Plan sent Germany through Belgium, bringing Britain in on 4 August
Historians disagree on blame: Fischer (German aims) versus Clark (Sleepwalkers, shared)

avoid: Alliances made war automatic

q: How did Europe carve up Africa so fast after 1880?

must.pt: The Berlin Conference of 1884-85 set rules for claims; most borders were drawn later in bilateral treaties
Quinine prophylaxis, steamboats, railways and the Maxim gun ('tools of empire', Headrick)
By 1914 only Ethiopia (victory at Adwa, 1896) and Liberia stayed independent
Leopold II's Congo Free State and its atrocities

avoid: Africa's borders were all drawn in one room in Berlin

q: Why was British India partitioned in 1947, and why was it so violent?

must.pt: The Muslim League's Lahore Resolution (1940) and Jinnah's demand for Pakistan after failed power-sharing talks
Mountbatten brought the handover forward to August 1947
Radcliffe drew the Punjab and Bengal lines in about five weeks and they were published only on 17 August, after independence
Some 10-20 million people moved and estimates of deaths range from about 200,000 to 2 million

avoid: Partition violence was ancient hatred

q: How did Tokugawa Japan stay at peace for 250 years?

must.pt: Victory at Sekigahara (1600) and the shogunate from 1603
Alternate attendance (sankin-kotai) kept daimyo and their families tied to Edo and spending
Hideyoshi's sword hunt (1588) and a fixed status order disarmed commoners
Foreign contact was restricted, not closed: the Dutch at Dejima, plus China, Korea via Tsushima, Ryukyu
It ended after Perry's ships (1853) and the Meiji Restoration (1868); Edo grew to about a million people

avoid: Japan was totally closed

q: Why did Qing China lose the Opium War?

must.pt: British East India Company opium from Bengal reversed the silver flow out of China
Lin Zexu destroyed about 20,000 chests of opium at Humen in 1839
Steam warships like the Nemesis and modern artillery overwhelmed Qing coastal defences
The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) ceded Hong Kong and opened five treaty ports

q: How did Islam spread so fast after 632?

must.pt: The Byzantine-Sasanian war of 602-628 and plague had exhausted both empires
Key victories: Yarmouk (636), Qadisiyya (636-37), Egypt (641), Nahavand (642)
By 711 Umayyad armies reached Iberia and the Indus
Conquest was fast but conversion slow: Muslims became a majority over centuries (Bulliet), with jizya on non-Muslims

avoid: Conversion by the sword as the main mechanism

q: Why did Buddhism almost vanish from India but thrive in East Asia?

must.pt: Ashoka's patronage and the Silk Road and sea routes carried it to Central, East and Southeast Asia
In India it lost royal patronage and was absorbed by devotional Hinduism (the Buddha as an avatar of Vishnu)
The great monasteries like Nalanda were sacked around 1193 (Bakhtiyar Khilji)
In China and Japan it adapted (Chan / Zen, Pure Land) and won state patronage

avoid: Islamic invasions alone ended Indian Buddhism

q: Did printing change Europe faster than it changed China and Korea?

must.pt: Woodblock printing in Tang China (Diamond Sutra, 868) and movable type by Bi Sheng about 1040
Korea's Jikji (1377) was printed with metal movable type before Gutenberg
Gutenberg's press about 1450 combined with an alphabet of a few dozen letters and many competing printers
Luther's pamphlets after 1517 show print's speed in Europe; the Ottoman world printed in Arabic script only from 1727 (Muteferrika)
Debate on how revolutionary print was: Eisenstein versus Adrian Johns

avoid: Gutenberg invented printing

q: Why did the Scientific Revolution happen in Europe and not in the Islamic world or China?

must.pt: Islamic and Chinese science were advanced: Ibn al-Haytham's optics, the Maragha school and the Tusi couple that Copernicus used
Copernicus (1543), Galileo, Newton's Principia (1687)
Explanations: printing, autonomous universities, competing states and the Republic of Letters (Mokyr)
The 'Needham question' itself is contested as a framing

avoid: Islamic science collapsed because of al-Ghazali (stated simply)

q: Why did Gothic cathedrals rise in twelfth-century France?

must.pt: Abbot Suger's choir at Saint-Denis (1144) is usually called the first Gothic building
Rib vaults, pointed arches and flying buttresses let walls open into stained glass
A theology of light (Suger's writings) shaped the look
Growing towns and farm surpluses paid for it; bishops competed (Chartres, Notre-Dame from 1163, Reims, Amiens)
Beauvais's choir collapsed in 1284: the style hit structural limits

q: How did written law codes evolve from Hammurabi to Justinian?

must.pt: Ur-Nammu's code (about 2100 BCE) is older than Hammurabi's
Hammurabi's stele (about 1754 BCE) set out case-style laws with penalties varying by social class
Rome's Twelve Tables (about 450 BCE) began written Roman law
Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis (529-534) compiled Roman law and, rediscovered in Bologna around 1070-1100, shaped European civil law

avoid: Hammurabi's was the first law code

q: How did horses and chariots change the ancient world?

must.pt: Ancient DNA shows the modern domestic horse came from the western steppe about 2200 BCE (Librado et al. 2021); Botai horses were not its ancestors
Spoked-wheel chariots appear with the Sintashta culture about 2000 BCE
Chariot warfare reached its height at Kadesh (1274 BCE)
Mounted cavalry and steppe peoples like the Scythians by the early first millennium BCE
Yamnaya steppe migrations about 3000 BCE are linked to the spread of Indo-European languages (Anthony, Reich)

q: How far did the Vikings travel, and what did they want?

must.pt: The raid on Lindisfarne (793) opened the Viking Age in the west
Rus traders went down the Volga and Dnieper to Constantinople and the Caliphate, as hoards of Arab silver dirhams show
Iceland about 870, Greenland about 985, and L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, with wood cut in 1021
Normandy was granted to Rollo in 911; Varangian Guard served the Byzantine emperor
They sought silver, slaves, land and trade

avoid: Horned helmets

q: How did Polynesians settle the Pacific?

must.pt: Lapita people reached Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by about 800 BCE
After a long pause, a fast expansion across East Polynesia about 1000-1200 CE; Aotearoa New Zealand last, about 1250-1300
Double-hulled voyaging canoes and wayfinding by stars, swells and birds
Sweet potato and genetic traces show contact with South America about 1200 (Ioannidis 2020)

avoid: Thor Heyerdahl: Polynesia was settled from South America

q: How did railways change how far you could travel in a day?

must.pt: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway (1830) was the first intercity line with steam only
A day's travel went from tens of kilometres by coach to several hundred by train
Transcontinental lines: the US in 1869, the Trans-Siberian from 1891 to 1916
Railway time and time zones (Britain 1847, North America 1883)
Prices converged between markets as freight costs fell

q: Why did the Classic Maya cities collapse?

must.pt: Southern lowland cities (Tikal, Copan, Calakmul) were largely abandoned in the Terminal Classic, about 800-950 CE
Lake and cave records show severe droughts in this period (Hodell, Haug, Kennett)
Endemic war between dynasties and the failure of divine kingship
Northern centres like Chichen Itza flourished afterward, and Maya people never disappeared

avoid: The Maya disappeared

q: Why was Angkor abandoned?

must.pt: Angkor was a vast low-density city (lidar shows about 1,000 km2) run on barays and canals
14th-15th century megadroughts alternating with intense monsoons damaged the water system (Buckley tree rings)
Ayutthaya sacked it in 1431 and the court moved toward Phnom Penh and sea trade
Angkor Wat was never fully abandoned; it stayed a Buddhist monastery

q: Who built Great Zimbabwe, and why was it abandoned?

must.pt: Built by ancestors of the Shona between about the 11th and 15th centuries
Its wealth came from cattle and gold and ivory traded to the coast through Sofala and Kilwa
It was abandoned by about 1450, probably as soils and pasture were exhausted and trade shifted north (Mutapa)
Colonial writers denied African builders; Rhodesia suppressed archaeologists who said otherwise

avoid: Phoenicians, Arabs or the Queen of Sheba built it

q: What do we actually know about why the Indus cities declined?

must.pt: The Mature Harappan phase ran about 2600-1900 BCE: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi
The script is undeciphered, so we have no written account
Decline was a gradual de-urbanisation after about 1900 BCE, with people moving east, not a sudden destruction
A weakening monsoon (the 4.2 ka event) and the Ghaggar-Hakra rivers drying are leading explanations
Wheeler's 'Aryan massacre' at Mohenjo-daro has been rejected

avoid: Aryan invaders destroyed the cities
Overconfident single-cause answer

q: Why did Columbus have to prove the Earth was round?

must.pt: Correct the premise: educated Europeans had known the Earth was a sphere since antiquity
Eratosthenes estimated its circumference about 240 BCE quite well
The real dispute was size: Columbus used too small an Earth and too wide an Asia, and his critics were right
The flat-Earth myth was spread in the 19th century, notably by Washington Irving (1828)

avoid: Accepting the premise
views: Jeffrey Burton Russell (Inventing the Flat Earth)

q: Who was in Vienna in 1913, and could they have met?

must.pt: Hitler lived in Vienna as a struggling painter until May 1913
Stalin spent several weeks in Vienna in early 1913 writing 'Marxism and the National Question'
Trotsky lived in Vienna from 1907 to 1914 editing Pravda
Freud practised at Berggasse 19; Tito worked near Vienna (Wiener Neustadt) in 1913
There is no evidence any of them met; overlap in time and city is not a meeting

avoid: Claims that they met
